title: Nalanda burned
hookLine: around 1200 the great monasteries were sacked and burned; the libraries were lost

cards: A Tibetan pilgrim walks into the ruins of Nalanda. His name is Dharmasvamin, and the account of his travels, written down by a student, describes what he found: halls damaged and deserted, most of the monks gone.

And in the middle of the ruins, an old teacher named Rahula Shribhadra, still teaching his students. Raiders had already come through. The account says they would come again while the pilgrim was there.

teach.h: A CHRONICLE: A FORT FULL OF BOOKS.
teach.b: First, the raids. As armies conquered northern India, they attacked the great monasteries of the east.
A Persian chronicle of the period describes soldiers storming what they took for a fortress, finding it full of books and shaven-headed men, and only afterward learning it had been a place of study.
Historians debate which monastery that passage describes, and whether Nalanda fell in one attack or was damaged over years.
Second, the libraries. These monasteries kept manuscripts copied by hand on palm leaf and bark, and later accounts say the libraries burned.

Some texts survived because monks carried them away, or because copies had already traveled to Tibet, Nepal or China. Some Buddhist works now survive only in translation, with no Sanskrit original known.
Monks were killed or scattered, and some fled north into the mountains, carrying what they could. Fourth, the witness. The pilgrim's account shows the place was not simply erased.
A teacher still taught. A student still came.

When the soldiers returned, the account says, the old teacher would not leave, so the pilgrim carried him on his back to a hiding place, and they waited until the danger passed. Then they went on with the lessons.
Here it is in smoke and ash: generations of learning gone, and an old teacher and his student, back at the books.

how: Buddhists remember the destruction of the great Indian monasteries in teaching and pilgrimage, and the ruins of Nalanda are visited today by pilgrims and students from across the Buddhist world.

practice: Think of something written or remembered that is gone, a letter thrown away, a recipe nobody wrote down, a grandparent's stories no one recorded, or a library you've only read about, and hold it gently in mind.
With each breath, honor it: the hands that made it, and the people who read it.

wordCard.voice: Nalanda burned. The raids that sacked the great monasteries of eastern India and burned their libraries, while some monks and some books escaped. Today's word.
